records.sourceFile: Association of social media use on sleep quality and performance among collegiate athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Watkins RA, Sugimoto D, Hunt D, Oldham J, Cacolice PA, Stracciolini A. Association of Social Media Use on Sleep Quality and Performance Among Collegiate Athletes. Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine. 2022;32(5):486-492.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study examined associations among objectively recorded social-media time, sleep disturbance, and competition results in NCAA Division III track-and-field and swimming athletes.
paper.tldr: Athletes using social media more than five hours per day reported worse sleep than those at two hours or less. Facebook time had a small association with competition outcomes, but total social-media time did not independently predict performance and the study cannot establish causation.
paper.methods: Eighty-seven athletes from two Division III colleges provided seven days of iPhone screen-time data and completed lifestyle and PROMIS sleep-disturbance measures. Athletes were grouped as no more than 2, more than 2 to 5, or more than 5 hours of daily social-media use; season or personal-best competition results were classified from public records and analyzed with adjustment for candidate confounders.
paper.findings: Mean social-media use was 4.6 ± 3.4 hours per day. The greater-than-5-hour group had worse sleep than the no-more-than-2-hour group (p=0.033). Greater Facebook time had a small adjusted association with not improving a season or personal best (adjusted OR 0.990, 95% CI 0.981-0.999), while total social-media time was not independently associated with the performance outcome.
paper.limitations: The cross-sectional design cannot establish causation. The sample came from two colleges and two sport settings, platform tracking was limited to iPhone use and selected applications, the performance outcome was coarse, and residual confounding and multiple comparisons make the Facebook finding uncertain.
paper.practicalImplications: Include digital habits in sleep and readiness conversations, especially when late or prolonged use coincides with poor sleep. Favor individualized routines, notification control, and protected wind-down time over a universal social-media ban.
paper.athleteDev: Teach athletes to review their own screen-time and sleep pattern, test a realistic pre-sleep routine, and evaluate whether the change improves sleep and next-day function rather than treating one platform as inherently performance-limiting.
paper.rtp: Social-media exposure is not a return-to-sport criterion. During rehabilitation, use sleep and digital routine as modifiable context alongside symptoms, training tolerance, and clinical progression.

records.sourceFile: Does it matter - Isometric or isokinetic assessment of quadriceps strength symmetry 9 months after ACLR in collegiate athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Cobian DG, Knurr KA, Joachim MR, Bednarek AL, Broderick AM, Heiderscheit BC. Does It Matter? Isometric or Isokinetic Assessment of Quadriceps Strength Symmetry 9 Months After ACLR in Collegiate Athletes. Sports Health. 2025;17(2):365-373.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study compared isometric and isokinetic quadriceps limb-symmetry indices and their relationships with functional kinetics and self-reported knee function in collegiate athletes approximately nine months after ACL reconstruction.
paper.tldr: Isometric and isokinetic symmetry agreed at the group level, but individual differences were wide enough that the modes should not be switched casually. Either can support testing when used consistently and interpreted with functional kinetics and athlete-reported status.
paper.methods: Thirty-five NCAA Division I athletes at 8.9 ± 2.5 months after ACL reconstruction completed isometric and isokinetic knee-extension testing on an isokinetic dynamometer, countermovement jumps, treadmill running, and the IKDC subjective knee form. Bland-Altman analysis assessed agreement, and correlations and regressions assessed relationships with knee kinetics and IKDC scores.
paper.findings: The mean difference between isokinetic and isometric strength symmetry was 1.0%, but 95% limits of agreement ranged from -25.1% to 23.0%. Isometric symmetry correlated moderately to strongly with running and jump kinetics (r=0.64-0.80), while isokinetic symmetry correlations were moderate (r=0.41-0.58). Both had weaker relationships with IKDC scores.
paper.limitations: The sample was small, narrow, and mostly bone-patellar tendon-bone autografts from one Division I setting. All testing used an isokinetic dynamometer, fatigue may have affected a long testing battery, and sex, sport, graft type, and concomitant procedures could not be fully examined.
paper.practicalImplications: Select the contraction mode that fits available equipment and the program's testing history, then keep it consistent across serial assessments. Interpret strength symmetry with absolute torque, movement kinetics, symptoms, confidence, and progressive sport exposure.
paper.athleteDev: Explain that an apparently similar group average does not make the two tests identical for one athlete. Show the athlete trends from the same protocol and connect those trends to functional tasks.
paper.rtp: Either isometric or isokinetic symmetry can contribute to an ACL return-to-sport battery, but neither is a stand-alone clearance test. Avoid comparing a current score with a prior score collected in the other mode.

records.sourceFile: Impact of Sled Loads on Performance and Kinematics of Elite Sprinters and Rugby Players.pdf

paper.citation: Pareja-Blanco F, Pereira LA, Reis VP, Fernandes V, Arruda AFS, Guerriero A, Alcaraz PE, Freitas TT, Loturco I. Impact of Sled Loads on Performance and Kinematics of Elite Sprinters and Rugby Players. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2022;17(3):465-473.
paper.abstract: This acute experimental study compared sprint velocity and lower-limb kinematics when elite sprinters and rugby-union players towed sleds loaded at fixed percentages of body mass.
paper.tldr: The same 20% and 60% body-mass sled loads did not create the same velocity or technical response in elite sprinters and rugby players. Sled prescription should be individualized by observed velocity decrement and mechanics, not body-mass percentage alone.
paper.methods: Eight elite male sprinters and ten male rugby-union players performed 20-m sprints with 0%, 20%, and 60% of body mass on their sport-specific surfaces. Timing splits were recorded over 0-5, 5-10, and 10-20 m, and an eight-sensor motion-analysis system measured stride length and hip, knee, and ankle angles.
paper.findings: Sprinters were faster unloaded and at 20% body mass, but group speed differences were no longer significant at 60%. Sprinters showed less velocity decrement than rugby players at 20% but more at 60%. Stride length did not differ consistently, while hip flexion and plantar-flexion responses differed by group and load.
paper.limitations: The acute cross-sectional comparison included only 18 elite men and tested 20 m. Sport-specific surface and footwear differed between groups, and the study did not establish longitudinal training effects, longer-distance transfer, or injury implications.
paper.practicalImplications: Choose a target velocity decrement and inspect sprint technique under load. Recalibrate sled mass when athlete, surface, footwear, or training phase changes rather than assuming the same body-mass percentage creates the same stimulus.
paper.athleteDev: Teach athletes that heavier is not automatically better and that the goal is a specific acceleration stimulus with acceptable mechanics. Use timing feedback to make the intended overload visible.
paper.rtp: For reconditioning, progress sled work by symptoms, velocity decrement, mechanics, and exposure tolerance. These healthy-athlete acute data do not define return-to-sprint or clearance thresholds.

records.sourceFile: Importance of Various Training-Load Measures in Injury Incidence of Professional Rugby League Athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Thornton HR, Delaney JA, Duthie GM, Dascombe BJ. Importance of Various Training-Load Measures in Injury Incidence of Professional Rugby League Athletes. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2017;12(6):819-824.
paper.abstract: This three-season cohort study examined how internal and external training-load features related to injury status across positions and individual professional rugby-league players.
paper.tldr: The load variables most associated with injury differed by position and athlete. The study supports individualized monitoring but does not provide universal workload thresholds or prove that a machine-learning alert prevents injury.
paper.methods: Daily training-load and injury-status data were collected from 25 National Rugby League players across the 2013-2015 seasons. Inputs included session-RPE load, total distance, high-speed-running distance, and high-metabolic-power distance across rolling windows and ratios. Generalized estimating equations and random forests were applied by position and athlete.
paper.findings: For adjustables, 7-day total distance and high-metabolic-power distance ranked highly; for hit-up forwards, session-RPE ratio and 14-day total distance were prominent; outside backs emphasized longer session-RPE windows, and wide-running forwards emphasized the session-RPE ratio. Individual models showed substantial variation in feature importance.
paper.limitations: The observational study involved one club and 25 players. Feature importance may be specific to that team's exposures, availability definition, and monitoring workflow; flexible individual models can overfit repeated data, and association with injury status cannot establish causal thresholds or prospective decision benefit.
paper.practicalImplications: Build monitoring around the athlete's role, history, and current capacity. Use load features to structure questions and multidisciplinary review, and prospectively test whether local alerts improve decisions before treating them as risk rules.
paper.athleteDev: Frame workload feedback as a shared planning tool rather than a prediction that an athlete will be injured. Pair the data with the athlete's symptoms, context, and training goals.
paper.rtp: Do not apply the paper's positional variables as return-to-sport cutoffs. During reconditioning, compare current exposures with the athlete's own staged plan, clinical status, and position demands.

records.sourceFile: Individual in-situ GPS derived accleration speed profiling - Toward automatization and refinement in male professional rugby union players.pdf

paper.citation: Miguens N, Brocherie F, Moulié L, Milhet P, Bon M, Lassus P, Toussaint JF, Sedeaud A. Individual In-Situ GPS-Derived Acceleration-Speed Profiling: Toward Automatization and Refinement in Male Professional Rugby Union Players. Sports Medicine - Open. 2024;10(1):6.
paper.abstract: This methodological study automated acceleration-speed profiling from routine GPS data and quantified profile reliability, measurement error, positional differences, and session-type differences in professional rugby union.
paper.tldr: Routine GPS data produced reliable-looking individual acceleration-speed profiles with automated outlier handling and explicit measurement error. The outputs are theoretical, data-quality dependent, and not validated as injury or return-to-sport decision rules.
paper.methods: Data from 49 male professional rugby-union players included 61.5 million GPS positions across 51 training sessions and 11 matches. Acceleration was derived from speed, density-based clustering removed atypical points, and linear profiles produced theoretical maximal acceleration, theoretical maximal speed, and slope. Two two-week phases were compared for reliability.
paper.findings: Every individual relationship was linear with R-squared above 0.81. Two-week ICCs ranged from 0.72 to 0.92 and SEM from 4.2% to 8.6%. Profiles differed by position and session type; matches tended to expose the highest theoretical acceleration while speed sessions exposed the highest theoretical speed.
paper.limitations: Results depend on GPS quality and acceleration derived from changes in speed rather than the embedded accelerometer. The intercepts are modeled rather than directly achieved maxima, the sample was one male professional setting, and no performance, injury, or return-to-sport outcome validation was performed.
paper.practicalImplications: Use routine data to supplement formal speed testing and to identify whether training and competition expose the athlete's profile. Display uncertainty and require changes to exceed measurement error before acting.
paper.athleteDev: Show athletes how different sessions expose acceleration and speed qualities, while explaining that the profile is an estimate shaped by the data captured rather than a fixed label of ability.
paper.rtp: A profile may help document exposure progression, but its theoretical values are not clearance criteria. Combine them with direct sprint testing, symptoms, tissue capacity, mechanics, and sport-specific task tolerance.

records.sourceFile: Inertial flywheel knee and hip dominant hamstring strength exercises in professional soccer players - Muscle use and velocity based eccentric overload.pdf

paper.citation: Suarez-Arrones L, Núñez FJ, Lara-Lopez P, Di Salvo V, Méndez-Villanueva A. Inertial Flywheel Knee- and Hip-Dominant Hamstring Strength Exercises in Professional Soccer Players: Muscle Use and Velocity-Based Mechanical Eccentric Overload. PLOS ONE. 2020;15(10):e0239977.
paper.abstract: This acute experimental study compared mechanical output and regional hamstring MRI responses to flywheel leg curl and conic-pulley hip extension in elite male professional soccer players.
paper.tldr: Flywheel leg curl and hip extension created different regional hamstring-use patterns, and eccentric overload depended on the metric and exercise. The acute MRI response can guide exercise emphasis but does not prove injury prevention or long-term adaptation.
paper.methods: Nineteen elite male professional soccer players were enrolled and 18 analyzed after assignment to flywheel leg curl (n=10) or conic-pulley hip extension (n=8). Athletes completed four sets of eight repetitions. Encoder measures quantified concentric and eccentric power, velocity, and time, while pre/post 3-T functional MRI T2 shifts assessed regional hamstring response.
paper.findings: Leg curl produced broader use of all four hamstring bellies and greater emphasis on semitendinosus and short-head biceps femoris. Hip extension emphasized proximal and medial long-head biceps femoris. Eccentric overload was observed for peak power in hip extension but was not consistently present across mean power, velocity, and exercise comparisons.
paper.limitations: The sample was small and unfamiliar with inertial devices, the study measured one acute session, and MRI T2 change is a metabolic proxy affected by tendon and elastic work. No longitudinal strength, hypertrophy, sprint, injury, or reinjury outcome was measured.
paper.practicalImplications: Select knee- and hip-dominant flywheel exercises according to the desired regional emphasis and movement role, provide familiarization, and monitor technique and output. Use a broader hamstring program rather than assuming one device supplies complete eccentric overload.
paper.athleteDev: Explain why two hamstring exercises may feel and load differently even when both are described as eccentric. Use objective output and tolerance to progress the exercise rather than chasing soreness.
paper.rtp: Regional emphasis may help exercise selection after hamstring injury, but the study does not establish reinjury protection or a lesion-specific protocol. Progress by healing status, symptoms, strength, sprint exposure, and sport function.

records.sourceFile: Do sports compression garments alter measures of peripheral blood flow - A systematic review with meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: O'Riordan SF, Bishop DJ, Halson SL, Broatch JR. Do Sports Compression Garments Alter Measures of Peripheral Blood Flow? A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Sports Medicine. 2023;53(2):481-501.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis evaluated whether sports compression garments change peripheral arterial or venous blood-flow measures at rest, during, immediately after, and in recovery from physiological challenges.
paper.tldr: Compression garments produced small changes in peripheral blood-flow measures, especially venous flow, but effects varied by timing and vessel type. A blood-flow surrogate should not be interpreted as proof of improved recovery or performance.
paper.methods: Twenty-two studies of healthy, active participants were included from 899 identified records. Twenty-three blood-flow measures were synthesized with random-effects models, and standardized mean differences were calculated by vessel type and timing relative to exercise or another physiological challenge.
paper.findings: Overall peripheral flow improved modestly (SMD 0.32, 95% CI 0.13-0.51), as did venous (0.37) and arterial (0.30) flow. During a challenge the pooled effect was 0.44; immediately afterward there was no overall change. In recovery, overall flow was not significant, although the venous subgroup improved while arterial flow did not.
paper.limitations: Studies varied across garments, applied pressure, timing, challenges, and 23 measurement methods. Participant and researcher blinding and pressure verification were often weak. The review team reported a research grant from 2XU, while stating that the manufacturer had no role in analysis or publication.
paper.practicalImplications: Compression garments may be offered as an optional, low-complexity strategy when fit, pressure, comfort, and timing are controlled. Judge usefulness by the athlete's target outcome and response, not by the proposed blood-flow mechanism alone.
paper.athleteDev: Set expectations that compression is an adjunct rather than a recovery substitute. Athletes should prioritize sleep, nutrition, hydration, and load management before relying on garments.
paper.rtp: Blood-flow changes in healthy participants are not return-to-sport criteria. Use garments only as a tolerated adjunct within the clinical and loading plan, not as evidence that tissue readiness has been restored.

records.sourceFile: Does resisted sprint training improve the sprint performance of field-based invasion team sport players - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Ward C, Ó Catháin C, Ní Chéilleachair N, Grassick S, Kelly DT. Does Resisted Sprint Training Improve the Sprint Performance of Field-Based Invasion Team Sport Players? A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2024;54(3):659-672.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis compared resisted and unresisted sprint training and examined how load and prescription method influenced sprint outcomes in field-based invasion-sport players.
paper.tldr: Resisted and unresisted sprinting improved sprint performance similarly. Resisted work was most useful for early acceleration, while no maximum-velocity improvement was detected, so it should complement rather than replace free sprinting.
paper.methods: Twenty-one studies were included after PRISMA-guided searches. Between-group analyses compared resisted with unresisted sprinting; within-group analyses estimated change in early acceleration, late acceleration, and maximum velocity. Subgroups examined external load and prescription by percentage velocity decrement.
paper.findings: Between-group analyses found no difference between resisted and unresisted sprint training across sprint phases. Resisted groups improved early acceleration (SMD -0.80) and late acceleration (-0.28) but not maximum velocity. Light and very heavy loads both improved early acceleration, and velocity-decrement prescription showed larger benefits than coarser load labels.
paper.limitations: Loading methods, sports, concurrent team training, interventions, and risk of bias varied. Favorable phase estimates often came from within-group change, while the direct comparison showed equivalence, and the evidence does not identify one universally optimal load.
paper.practicalImplications: Use resisted sprinting when the goal is acceleration-specific overload and retain adequate unresisted and maximum-velocity sprint exposure. Prescribe and monitor the actual velocity decrement rather than body-mass percentage or a light/heavy label alone.
paper.athleteDev: Help athletes connect sled load with the intended acceleration quality and technical response. Stop adding load when velocity loss or mechanics no longer match the session goal.
paper.rtp: Resisted sprinting can be one graded reconditioning tool, but these training studies do not define injury-specific progression or clearance. Advance alongside free sprinting, symptoms, mechanics, and exposure tolerance.

records.sourceFile: Efects of Warm‑Up, Post‑Warm‑Up, and Re‑Warm‑Up Strategies on Explosive Eforts in Team Sports- A Systematic Review.pdf

paper.citation: Silva LM, Neiva HP, Marques MC, Izquierdo M, Marinho DA. Effects of Warm-Up, Post-Warm-Up, and Re-Warm-Up Strategies on Explosive Efforts in Team Sports: A Systematic Review. Sports Medicine. 2018;48(10):2285-2299.
paper.abstract: This systematic review examined warm-up content and strategies for preserving or restoring explosive performance during the delay before play and at halftime in team sports.
paper.tldr: Short, progressive, sport-specific warm-ups with explosive tasks generally supported sprint, jump, and agility performance. When athletes must wait, heat retention and brief re-warm-ups may preserve readiness, but protocol heterogeneity prevents one universal formula.
paper.methods: Thirty articles published from 1981 through August 2017 met inclusion criteria after searches of four databases. The authors assessed risk of bias and recalculated Cohen's d for warm-up, post-warm-up, and re-warm-up strategies affecting explosive team-sport efforts.
paper.findings: Examples included improved sprint performance after eight 60-m efforts and improved sprint, jump, and agility after dynamic activity following jogging. Heated garments outperformed passive rest in some transitions, while brief explosive re-warm-ups were most useful when delays exceeded 15 minutes and at halftime. The authors proposed a generally shorter 10-15 minute progressive warm-up.
paper.limitations: Protocols, intensities, durations, recovery periods, control groups, sports, and outcomes varied widely. Several recommendations came from single studies, and the heterogeneity prevented meta-analysis or a definitive optimal protocol across populations.
paper.practicalImplications: Design the warm-up backward from the first competitive demands and the expected delay before play. Preserve temperature during unavoidable inactivity and use a brief explosive re-warm-up when rules, space, and athlete readiness allow.
paper.athleteDev: Give athletes a simple personal warm-up and re-warm-up menu that they can execute reliably under travel, bench, and halftime constraints, while retaining the team's common structure.
paper.rtp: Reintegrate warm-up and re-warm-up demands progressively during return to sport. The review does not provide injury-specific readiness thresholds, so pair explosive preparation with clinical and exposure criteria.

records.sourceFile: Effect of movement velocity during      resistance training on dynamic muscular strength - A systematic review    and   meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Davies TB, Kuang K, Orr R, Halaki M, Hackett D. Effect of Movement Velocity During Resistance Training on Dynamic Muscular Strength: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Medicine. 2017;47(8):1603-1617.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis compared fast or explosive with moderate-slow resistance-training repetitions when prescribed intensity and volume were matched.
paper.tldr: Fast and moderate-slow repetitions produced similar dynamic-strength gains overall. Faster movement at moderate loads showed only a small nonsignificant trend, so velocity should be selected for the exercise and adaptation goal rather than treated as universally superior.
paper.methods: Fifteen comparative studies involving 509 participants aged 19-73 years met the criteria. Programs lasted at least four weeks, compared fast with moderate-slow isotonic training under matched prescribed intensity and volume, and measured dynamic strength. Subgroups examined intensity, age, and training status.
paper.findings: Strength gains were similar when all intensities were pooled. At moderate intensities of 60-79% 1RM, faster training showed a small favorable trend (effect size 0.31, p=0.06). Age and training status did not explain a clear difference between velocities.
paper.limitations: Loading, actual velocity, age, training status, exercise selection, and intervention duration varied substantially. More than half the interventions lasted only six to eight weeks, athlete-specific evidence was limited, and the moderate-load result did not reach conventional significance.
paper.practicalImplications: Program repetition intent and speed alongside load, range of motion, fatigue, and technical quality. Use fast intent where power and rapid force expression matter, while recognizing that controlled slower work can still build strength.
paper.athleteDev: Teach athletes that repetition speed is a programming variable, not a contest. The correct speed is the one that matches the load, exercise, and session goal while maintaining control.
paper.rtp: Select movement velocity according to healing, symptoms, load tolerance, and the next functional demand. The review does not support a single velocity threshold for return-to-sport progression.

records.sourceFile: Effects of acute sleep deprivation on sporting performance in athletes - A comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Gong M, Sun M, Sun Y, Jin L, Li S. Effects of Acute Sleep Deprivation on Sporting Performance in Athletes: A Comprehensive Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Nature and Science of Sleep. 2024;16:935-948.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis quantified the effects of acute whole-night and partial sleep deprivation on multiple categories and times of athletic performance.
paper.tldr: Acute sleep deprivation impaired athletic performance overall, with larger pooled effects for high-intensity intermittent work and skill control. Heterogeneous and sparse subgroups mean the exact effect size and time-of-day pattern should not be treated as a universal rule.
paper.methods: Twenty-seven studies contributing 75 performance indicators were synthesized using Stata. Analyses estimated overall performance effects, compared whole-night and partial deprivation timing, grouped outcomes by athletic ability, and compared morning with afternoon performance after acute sleep deprivation.
paper.findings: The overall effect was -0.56. Reported effects were -1.57 for high-intensity intermittent exercise, -1.06 for skill control, -0.67 for speed, -0.54 for aerobic endurance, and -0.39 for explosive power. Late-night or early-morning sleep loss and afternoon testing produced larger estimates in selected subgroup analyses.
paper.limitations: Underlying studies varied in quality, deprivation protocol, athlete population, and outcome. Some subgroups contained very few indicators, outcome classification was debatable, and multiple indicators from studies may create more apparent precision than the independent evidence supports.
paper.practicalImplications: Protect sleep before high-intensity, speed, skill, and decision-critical sessions. When acute loss is unavoidable, consider lowering complexity or dose, increasing monitoring, and rescheduling the most consequential work when feasible.
paper.athleteDev: Build a practical sleep-loss plan before travel or schedule disruption: report the loss honestly, avoid compensating with reckless training or stimulant use, and coordinate adjustments with staff.
paper.rtp: Acute sleep loss can reduce the quality of rehabilitation and testing. If readiness is clearly impaired, interpret performance tests cautiously and adjust the session rather than mistaking fatigue for tissue or skill capacity.

records.sourceFile: Effects of bilateral and unilateral resistance training on horizontally orientated movement performance - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Moran J, Ramirez-Campillo R, Liew B, Chaabene H, Behm DG, García-Hermoso A, Izquierdo M, Granacher U. Effects of Bilateral and Unilateral Resistance Training on Horizontally Orientated Movement Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2021;51(2):225-242.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis compared bilateral and unilateral resistance-training effects on sprinting and other horizontally oriented movement outcomes.
paper.tldr: Both bilateral and unilateral training improved horizontal movement performance, and neither was superior overall. Programming can use both according to loading capacity, stability, symptoms, and movement goals.
paper.methods: Eleven studies met inclusion criteria. Random-effects meta-analyses calculated standardized mean differences for short sprint and related horizontal movement outcomes, comparing bilateral with unilateral programs and exploring training type, duration, frequency, experience, and other moderators.
paper.findings: Bilateral training improved performance with an SMD of 0.60 and unilateral training with an SMD of 0.57. The direct difference was nonsignificant (SMD 0.17, 95% CI -0.15 to 0.50), with moderate heterogeneity. Combined strength-plus-plyometric approaches tended to produce larger effects than strength-only programs.
paper.limitations: Programs and outcomes varied, between-study heterogeneity was moderate, and moderator analyses split continuous variables and tested factors independently. Those choices limit power and cannot account for interactions among load, exercise, experience, and program design.
paper.practicalImplications: Use a multidimensional program that includes bilateral and unilateral work. Let absolute-load needs, stability, equipment, movement direction, athlete preference, and response determine the balance rather than assuming specificity makes unilateral work superior.
paper.athleteDev: Explain that bilateral and unilateral exercises solve different programming problems and both can transfer to movement. Progress quality and loading instead of treating one category as more athletic.
paper.rtp: Unilateral work may help grade side-specific loading and bilateral work may restore higher absolute force, but neither mode is a clearance test. Select and progress both according to symptoms, capacity, mechanics, and sport demands.
